{{Short description|British mathematician (1920–2011)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2021}}
'''Frank Featherstone Bonsall''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]]<ref name=biomem>{{Cite journal|last=Gillespie|first=T. A.|date=2020|title=Frank Featherstone Bonsall. 31 March 1920 – 22 February 2011|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=69|pages=63–77|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2020.0007|s2cid=222142931|doi-access=free}}</ref> (31 March 1920, [[Crouch End]], [[London]] – 22 February 2011,<ref>{{cite journal |title=Obituaries |journal=University of Oxford Gazette |volume=141 |issue=4947 |date=10 March 2011 |page=500}}</ref> [[Harrogate]]) was a British [[mathematician]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/comment/obituaries/frank-bonsall-1.1094739 |title=Frank Bonsall &#124; Herald Scotland |access-date=16 November 2011 |archive-date=16 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150116161314/http://www.heraldscotland.com/comment/obituaries/frank-bonsall-1.1094739 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Bonsall was born on 31 March 1920, the youngest son of Wilfred C Bonsall and Sarah Frank. His older brother was [[Arthur Bonsall]].<ref name="auto">{{MacTutor|id=Bonsall}}</ref> He married Gillian Patrick, a [[Somerville College, Oxford|Somerville]] graduate, in 1947.<ref name=MCreg /> Bonsall and his wife were keen hill-walkers.<ref name=biomem/> He wrote two articles for The Scottish Mountaineering Club on the definition of a [[Munro]]. After his retirement, Bonsall and his wife moved to Harrogate.

==Career==
Bonsall graduated from [[Bishop's Stortford College]] in 1938, and studied at [[Merton College, Oxford]].<ref name="MCreg">{{cite book|editor1-last=Levens|editor1-first=R.G.C.|title=Merton College Register 1900–1964|date=1964|publisher=Basil Blackwell|location=Oxford|page=290}}</ref>
He served in [[World War II]], in the [[Corps of Royal Engineers]], and in India from 1944 to 1946.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Bonsall/|archiveurl=https://archive.today/20120731055029/http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Bonsall.html|url-status=dead|title=Frank Bonsall - Biography|website=Archive.today|archive-date=31 July 2012|access-date=29 October 2021}}</ref>

He lectured at the [[University of Edinburgh]] from 1947 to 1948; was visiting associate professor at [[Oklahoma State University]] from 1950 to 1951; taught at [[Newcastle University]], with [[Werner Wolfgang Rogosinski]] in the 1950s. He taught at the [[University of Edinburgh]], from 1963 to 1984.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-frank-bonsall-leading-mathematician-of-the-postwar-years-who-led-research-into-functional-analysis-2261207.html| title= Professor Frank Bonsall: Leading mathematician of the post-war years who led research into functional analysis| author=Alastair Gillespie| date=4 April 2011| work=The Independent}}</ref> In 1963, a second chair in Mathematics was established (the Maclaurin chair). Bonsall took up the chair in 1965, but spent the following year as a visiting professor at Yale.<ref name="auto"/> In 1966, he was awarded the [[London Mathematical Society]]'s [[Berwick Prize]].

Despite not himself having a PhD, Bonsall supervised many PhD candidates<ref>{{mathgenealogy|15633}}</ref> who knew him affectionately as "FFB".

*''Compact linear operators'', Yale University, Dept. of Mathematics, 1967
*Frank F. Bonsall, John Duncan, [https://books.google.com/books/about/Numerical_Ranges_of_Operators_on_Normed.html?id=HOQ6AAAAIAAJ ''Numerical ranges of operators and normed spaces and of all elements of normed algebras''], London Mathematical Society, 1971
*Frank F. Bonsall, J. Duncan, [https://books.google.com/books/about/Numerical_Ranges_II.html?id=BD44AAAAIAAJ ''Numerical ranges II''], Cambridge univ. press, 1973
*Frank F. Bonsall, J. Duncan, ''Complete normed algebras'', 1973<ref>{{cite journal|author=Rickart, C. E.|authorlink=Charles Earl Rickart|title=Review: ''Complete normed algebras'' by F. F.
